title: We Asked 8 Sommeliers: What’s the Most Overrated White Wine? (2026)
summary:
White wine is a reliable go-to for many drinkers. It can bring crisp, saline edges, juicy tropical fruit notes, or even rich, nutty flavors. For its diversity, palatability, and low-ABV nature, the genre has recently seen a boost in appeal. But along with that growing popularity, some grapes, regions, or bottles tend to take more than their fair share of the spotlight. And the bottles that drum up the most excitement might not always be all they are hyped up to be.

content:
White wine is a reliable go-to for many drinkers. It can bring crisp, saline edges, juicy tropical fruit notes, or even rich, nutty flavors. For its diversity, palatability, and low-ABV nature, the genre has recently seen a boost in appeal.

But along with that growing popularity, some grapes, regions, or bottles tend to take more than their fair share of the spotlight. And the bottles that drum up the most excitement might not always be all they are hyped up to be. Consumers each have their own preferences, but sometimes it’s worth looking past the wines receiving major recognition to discover a new hidden gem.

That’s why we tapped eight sommeliers from around the country to name the white wines they think are the most overrated. From a certain Loire Valley region that many consider overpriced to butter-bomb Chardonnays, here’s what they had to say.

The most overrated white wines, according to sommeliers:

  • Sancerre
  • Go-to white wines
  • Pinot Grigio
  • Buttery California Chardonnay
  • Muscat
  • Yellow Tail Chardonnay
  • Pinot Gris

“The most overrated white wine has to be Sancerre — not because it is not one of the most famously delicious expressions of Sauvignon Blanc known to the world for centuries, but because there are so many other wonderful things coming from the Loire Valley. Menatou Salon often offers Sauvignon Blancs that, in my opinion, drink closer to Sancerre these days than one may want to believe (Domaine Pellé’s Morogues Blanc, for example). Sancerre sets the stage and creates a wonderful point of departure for a world of crisp citrus and mineral-driven white wines that can also be found in Austria, Italy, and many other white wine growing regions of France. We are always happy to help Sancerre drinkers find an alternative they never knew they loved.” —Sam Stresing, wine director, Lowland, Charleston, S.C.

“The most overrated white wine isn’t a particular grape or region, but the one you choose on autopilot. I’m a big believer in drinking whatever you love, but we give the same handful of whites far too much attention when there’s an entire world of incredible wines out there. I love Chardonnay as much as the next girl, but give Godello a chance!” —Emily Nevin-Giannini, senior beverage director, Barcelona Wine Bar, Norwalk, Conn.

“Pinot Grigio is the most overrated white wine. There are some not-so-great representations out there that get outsized attention. But fear not! There are some awesome wines made from Pinot Grigio from all over the world, including Italy, the U.S., Australia, New Zealand, and France!” —Barb Werley, master sommelier, Nuri Steakhouse, Dallas

“I’m more drawn to crisp, refreshing flavors like green apple and citrus, with stainless steel or neutral oak aging that keeps the wine balanced and easy to drink. I’m happy to see the trend moving away from the heavy, buttery California Chardonnays that were so popular for years. Sometimes all that oak can overpower the fruit, so it’s nice to see more wineries letting the wine speak for itself and keeping things fresh.” —Austin Krudys, beverage manager, The Chloe, Nashville

“Muscat and its related varieties (Moscatel, Moscato, etc.) have a long history of producing beautiful wines across a range of styles, from the Mediterranean to Japan. Personally, though, I often find the pronounced white floral aromas overpowering, making this a grape family I tend not to gravitate toward. That’s a matter of personal taste rather than a reflection of the quality or diversity of these wines.” —Sarah MacIsaac, wine director, Nautilus Pier 4, Boston

“As of October 2026, the world’s most overrated white wine has to be Sancerre. Production has been pushed to the max in order to meet demand, significantly diluting quality while prices have continued to increase. (But I can’t exactly blame producers for trying to capitalize on the Sancerre craze). Outside of a few key producers like Vatan, the wine is decidedly mediocre, especially when you consider the universe of other great white wines available: Vinho Verde, Albariño, Aussie Riesling, Willamette Valley Chardonnay, South African Chenin. I could go on forever.” —Evan White, wine director, Bludorn Hospitality, Houston

“Yellow Tail Chardonnay is a classic example of brand recognition doing more work than the wine itself. It’s familiar, inexpensive, and easy to find, but ‘familiar’ isn’t the same as ‘good.’ Spend a couple of dollars more, and you can usually find a Chardonnay with brighter acidity, cleaner fruit, better balance, and less heavy oak or residual sweetness … something more refreshing, distinctive, and food-friendly than this soft crowd-pleaser.” —Emelio Sansone, executive chef, Tin Lizzie Lounge, Seattle

“At the moment, the most overrated white wine is Pinot Gris. I would much rather guide a guest to a variety of other aromatic whites ranging from Riesling to Zibibbo depending on their stylistic preferences. There’s just so much more interesting wine available to try.” —William Jones, chief operating officer and wine director, Deep Roots Restaurant Group, Fairhope, Ala.

content:
India Pale Ales are the darling of the United States craft brewing industry. The style is the most produced among U.S. craft brewers, accounting for roughly 50 percent of the segment’s off-premise sales and 40 percent of its volume, according to Circana and the Brewers Association, respectively. With sub-styles ranging from New England hazies to crisp, bitter West Coast expressions, the hoppy category leaves room for innovation and experimentation.

Given Americans’ general infatuation with these flavor-blasted brews — which can land anywhere from piny and resinous to juicy and citrusy — we parsed through BeerAdvocate’s database to find the highest-rated IPA in each state this year. As a baseline, we only considered beers with over 100 ratings on the platform for this list.

Out of the many IPA sub-categories, hazy — including hazy imperial — had the strongest showing as the highest-rated IPA in 19 states. title: Ask a Bartender: Is There a ‘Right’ Way to Split the Check?
summary:
Contemporary bargoers — particularly Gen Z drinkers — have recently been called out for their lack of etiquette around paying the bill. Some reports suggest they don’t open tabs, which can interrupt a bartender’s flow, closing out tabs left and right instead of processing a single transaction at the end of the night. Another common paying practice recently called into question is requesting to split the check. As consumers pinch their pennies and keep their cash close to their chests, many are reluctant to put their cards down for an entire table’s worth of food and drinks.

The article Ask a Bartender: Is There a ‘Right’ Way to Split the Check? appeared first on VinePair.
content:
Contemporary bargoers — particularly Gen Z drinkers — have recently been called out for their lack of etiquette around paying the bill. Some reports suggest they don’t open tabs, which can interrupt a bartender’s flow, closing out tabs left and right instead of processing a single transaction at the end of the night.

Another common paying practice recently called into question is requesting to split the check. As consumers pinch their pennies and keep their cash close to their chests, many are reluctant to put their cards down for an entire table’s worth of food and drinks. Instead, certain groups like to split a check, either evenly or item-by-item, to keep things “easy” and “fair.”

What’s “easy” and “fair” for customers isn’t always the case for those on the other side of the transaction. To better understand the proper paying etiquette, VinePair tapped former bar owner and Luxardo brand ambassador Laura Newman and bartender Ashtyn “Ash” Harris to lay out the do’s and don’ts of splitting the tab.

Overall, both pros agree that splitting the bill is generally an acceptable request. Most modern point-of-sale (POS) systems, such as Toast and Square, can do the dividing and itemizing automatically and ease the bartender’s job. While splitting a check into individual tabs may take servers a few extra minutes — and, in turn, inconvenience them during a busy service — the task has become a normal part of the job.

“I have no problem splitting a tab,” Newman says. “At the end of the day, I always keep in mind that hospitality comes first, and even if it’s during a high-volume night where I’m trying to get things done quickly, the job is to make the guests feel welcome.”

Harris agrees that splitting checks is par for the course, albeit time consuming. What irks her, however, is when larger groups that order a host of different dishes and drinks ask for a divided check. In large-group cases, she says best practice is to inform the bartender or server ahead of time that they’ll want individual checks.

“A group of six asking for split, itemized checks is what grinds my gears, especially if they did not mention that prior to ordering,” Harris, who works behind the stick at esteemed cocktail bar Press Club in Washington, D.C., says. “For large groups, I try to keep an organized tab by seat number to make separate checks easier.”

No matter how time consuming, Newman and Harris will both execute the request if the group asks for it. That said, while there is no set form of etiquette for splitting tabs, Newman says it’s up to the guests’ discretion to measure how inconvenient a split check would be for bartenders. If a group deems the request too disruptive to the server’s workflow they should opt to put one person’s card down and do the splitting themselves.

“A group of three might ask, ‘I had these three drinks, my friend had three different drinks, and the two of us are going to split an order of tater tots, but the three of us are going to split the nachos,’” Newman says. “I can split that, but at that point, just Venmo.”

For checks with low totals, groups of friends should also consider implementing the old-school rule of “I’ll cover this one, and you get the next one.” At some point in a relationship, it’s just easier to call it even over time rather than dissecting each and every bill.

Splitting checks doesn’t necessarily impact a bartender’s tips, but the pause to their flow could compromise other sales, Newman says. If a server spends a long time closing out each individual of a large group — time that could have been dedicated to serving different guests — other tables may feel overlooked and tip less.

Regardless of how annoying the request may be or how it may sacrifice sales, both Harris and Newman express they can’t dictate how a group chooses to pay their check.

“I can’t tell guests how to pay their tab,” Harris says, “but I do love the guest who covers the check because they want points on their card, or because they know how to use Venmo or Cash App, etc.”

title: 10 Bars and Restaurants That Defined the Modern Martini
summary:
Cocktail trends come and go, but the Martini is forever. People might debate whether its eternal presence hinges on its flavor or how it makes one feel, but it doesn’t matter in the end. If society ever decides to turn its back on the Martini, humanity’s demise will likely soon follow. But it’s not all about the aesthetics, the Martini is also deceptively complex. It doesn’t look complicated, given its appearance as clear-to-opaque liquid in a Nick & Nora or its eponymous V-shaped glass.

The article 10 Bars and Restaurants That Defined the Modern Martini appeared first on VinePair.
content:
Cocktail trends come and go, but the Martini is forever. People might debate whether its eternal presence hinges on its flavor or how it makes one feel, but it doesn’t matter in the end. If society ever decides to turn its back on the Martini, humanity’s demise will likely soon follow.

But it’s not all about the aesthetics, the Martini is also deceptively complex. It doesn’t look complicated, given its appearance as clear-to-opaque liquid in a Nick & Nora or its eponymous V-shaped glass. Yet inside each vessel is a melange of ritual, science, historic nuance, and bartending artistry, with the occasional dash of personal preference thrown in for good measure. This makes the drink surprisingly intimidating — I’ve had a few bartenders over the years confess to me that making a Martini à la minute based on customer-driven specs is the most nerve-racking part of their job.

These elements also keep the drink from being static. The Martini is fertile ground for subtle evolution, and these changes simply expand the possibilities of the Martini-drinking experience as opposed to merely creating “riffs on a classic” (even though riffs on the classic do indeed exist and are noteworthy). The hospitality industry naturally serves as the prime mover behind the Martini’s shape-shifting abilities. And over the past few years there have been a few bars and restaurants that have particularly enhanced the complexity of how we define the modern Martini.

Here, we chart out 10 Martinis that helped shape how we understand the cocktail today. Created as original recipes or specific specs at great bars across the globe, these provided the inspiration behind a countless number of Martini styles and variations — from the popularization of the sidecar to the Martini that launched a thousand super savory riffs. No one contribution is greater than the other, so it’s pointless to try to discuss the following establishments in terms of a hierarchy. It’s best to simply appreciate how they all played a part in progressing the Martini’s perpetually ongoing narrative.

The Martini as a Destination Drink
Venue: Dukes Bar

Initially created in 1985 by bartender Salvatore Calabrese, a Dukes Martini consists of roughly 5 ounces of high-proof freezer gin served at a piercingly cold temperature into a vermouth-rinsed glass. It’s so famous, it spawned its own self-named Martini subcategory. It also transformed the Martini into a drink worth traveling to a specific location to enjoy. There’s a distinct difference between enjoying a Dukes Martini and enjoying a martini at Dukes, and this has everything to do with being immersed in the sense of place that pulses through this hotel bar tucked within a secluded slice of London’s Mayfair district. The Martinis are great, of course, but the vibe is the drink’s defining element.

A Bartending Legend Revives Orange Bitters
Venue: The Rainbow Room

Orange bitters were an integral part of the earliest Martini recipes, but they all but disappeared from both the drink and the market by the early ’90s. Their near-extinction didn’t sit well with legendary bartender Gary “Gaz” Regan. Rather than griping about their disappearance, he set out to revive the category by making his own orange bitters based on a recipe he found in a 1946 book called “The Gentleman’s Companion.” He shared his early iterations with a few of his bartending friends; one of the recipients was none other than Dale DeGroff, who began playing around with them at The Rainbow Room (which presumably meant dropping them into a Martini, given DeGroff’s knack of reviving original cocktail recipes). Eventually, Regan found a recipe he liked and partnered with the Sazerac Company in 2005 to sell his creation as Regan’s Orange Bitters No. 6. The new bottle gave the bartenders of the fledgling craft cocktail scene a new element to introduce into their own Martini schemes.

The Martini Gets Its Sidecar
Venue: Pegu Club

A Martini is best served — and enjoyed — cold. Science causes chaos and disruption to this beautiful principle: The longer the Martini sits in the glass, the warmer and less delicious it gets. Martini drinkers dealt with this sad reality for decades until Audrey Saunders changed the game in the early 2000s. At her seminal New York bar Pegu Club, Saunders started serving guests half-pours of their Martinis in the glass while the other half chilled in a small carafe ensconced in ice. It kept the Martini experience appropriately cold from start to finish. Though Saunders isn’t credited with inventing the concept of a sidecar, she did incite its modern resurgence; the tactic proliferated throughout the New York City bar scene, most notably through key bartending figures like Julie Reiner.

Martinis Made with Theatrical Flair
Venue: The Connaught Bar

The Martini is a ritualistic drink at its core, but its customs are traditionally personal and meted out through individualized specs. The Connaught Bar in London augmented this ritual by incorporating its own sense of ceremonial showmanship when the hotel bar debuted its Martini table cart service in 2008. After guests participated in the liquid liturgy by selecting core elements like gin and bitters, bartenders stretched one hand upward and poured the drink from high above the glass, expressing the stream with a lemon peel with their free hand. It looked like the bartending equivalent of a musician playing a theremin, and it pushed the artistry behind the routine of Martini preparation to its fullest, most captivating extent. The Martini cart concept is widespread these days, and some bars and restaurants use it as a stage for flashy pour techniques. Those that do owe a debt to Connaught’s penchant for flair.

The Martini Riff Gets Serious
Venue: Dear Irving

At the end of the 2000s, Martini riffs were still largely defined by wannabes like the Appletini and the Lemon Drop Martini. Then Meaghan Dorman got behind the stick at Raines Law Room in 2009, started whipping up Gibsons, and reminded everyone what a real Martini riff looked like. Five years later at Dear Irving, she successfully executed a riff on a riff, replacing the drink’s traditional dry vermouth with white (bianco) vermouth to give the cocktail a slightly sweeter profile. The wannabes are still out there, and to be fair, they can be good when properly made (exhibit A: the Espresso Martini). But they now must share the spotlight with legit Martini variations thanks in part to Dorman’s handiwork.

The House Martini Levels Up
Venue: Maison Premiere

The notion of a house Martini is nothing new to the American bar scene. However, it feels fair to say Brooklyn’s Maison Premiere pushed the limits to what a house Martini may look like when it introduced its signature Old King Cole Martini around 2015. They served the drink tableside with an elaborate presentation, providing the first indication that this wasn’t a basic beverage. The specs backed up this signal: High proof, freezer-cold Old Raj gin, extra-dry vermouth, and three dashes of orange bitters, garnished with a lemon twist and Castelvetrano olives. Everything about the drink felt more special than a house Martini deserved to be. Order one now, and that feeling is still present.

The Freezer Door Martini Revival
Venue: Dante

Freezer door Martinis were popular during the mid-20th century, but practically disappeared during the disco drink era. It seemed poised for a comeback during the craft cocktail revival in retrospect, if only because the idea of sticking a batched bunch of pre-diluted Martinis in a freezer seems like a no-brainer. It just needed a champion with a large enough platform. Dante not only had that stage, the bar expanded it to an amphitheatre with the introduction of its Martini Happy Hour in 2015, giving guests the chance to enjoy a piercingly cold drink for $10. While there’s little reason to believe the freezer Martini revival wasn’t going down in other parts of the country, Dante’s doings gave the trend the push it needed to fully go mainstream. Nowadays, it’s not unusual to walk into a cocktail bar and see them straining the limits of their icebox to achieve maximum Martini chilliness.

Martinis Get a Savory Spin
Venue: Bonnie’s

Dirty Martinis have been around since the dawn of the 20th century, and they traditionally contained the same type of dirt (olive brine). While this made the concept consistent, it also left a lot of room for innovation. In 2022, the Brooklyn’s Cantonese American restaurant Bonnie’s leaned hard into that empty space when it launched its signature MSG Martini, a variant that added the unfairly-maligned flavor enhancer and shaoxing wine along with the usual olive brine. The result was a Martini of Bob Saget-levels of dirtiness, and it not only helped push the limits of what a Dirty Martini can be, it also kick-started the burgeoning savory cocktail trend into overdrive. It’s not too hard to find a Dirty Martini whose profile reads more like a snack than a drink, as flavors ranging from sour cream and onion to crispy chicken skin are on the table.

The Martini as a Holistic Experience
Venue: Le Veau D’Or

The Martini can be such an intensely personal cocktail, it may be difficult for guests to deviate from personal preference. While Martini experimentation obviously occurred during the craft cocktail revival era, convincing those set in their ways to try something new was a tricky proposition. When NYC’s legendary French bistro Le Veau D’Or reopened in 2024, it took a unique approach to this conundrum by offering two Martini options. The “Martini Your Way” allowed guests to stay in their comfort zone. The “Martini Our Way,” on the other hand, is a riff involving a sidecar of vermouth and sparkling water chilled by Martini-soaked ice. The duo encouraged patrons to color outside their lines, but also reassured them their own specs were just as good. It set the template for bars to take a gentle approach to guiding guests through Martini drinking — one that’s beginning to become more commonplace.

The Martini Glass Swap
Venue: Hillstone Restaurant Group

The Hillstone Restaurant Group is a restaurant collective known for its upscale-yet-approachable chain eateries with locations across the country. It’s also the most unlikely place to run into one of the Martini world’s coolest innovations, the glass swap: About halfway through a guest’s Martini session, the bartender will pour the remainder of the drink into a freshly chilled glass. Nobody knows when the venues in Hillstone’s gastronomic empire started doing this simple yet oh-so-effective tactic — the company tends to be mum about its operations — but some people guestimate it’s been a thing for a couple decades. Regardless of what it actually did start, the swap’s ability to astonish and delight amid such unexpected surroundings continues to endure. These days, a lot of the “cool kids” (read: Places on all of the “best bars” lists) are pulling off this tactic, which makes it even more fun to think that a chain restaurant group kicked off the trend.

 

*Header image photos retrieved from Maison Premiere, The Connaught Bar, and Dukes London

content:
This is VinePair’s Booze News Weekly Roundup, where we gather the hottest headlines and product releases every Friday for a snapshot of what’s happening in the beverage alcohol industry. This week, we have updates on Diageo’s toxic chemical spill, SCOTUS to review a home distilling case, the latest product releases, and more.

News to know:

  • Diageo’s toxic spill contaminates “pristine” Scottish river: The water in Scotland’s River Spey was once some of the cleanest in the world until a chemical spill from Diageo’s Cardhu Distillery. Contamination from the incident killed thousands of salmon, trout, and other fish. The Scottish Environment Protection Agency (SEPA) is actively investigating Diageo to see how the caustic soda, the toxic contaminant, entered the waters. A Diageo spokesperson told Bloomberg that the company is complying with SEPA and helping plan regeneration and restoration measures.
  • Supreme Court agrees to hear ban on home distilling case: Supreme Court decided on Monday to hear the case that will determine if the 1868 federal ban on home distilling is unconstitutional. The justices reached the decision following a request for review from Trump’s Department of Justice, which it filed after the SCOTUS had put a delay on deciding whether or not to hear the case. Hearings will begin as early as January.
  • Fawn Weaver motions to block Uncle Nearest sale: As three potential buyers eye Uncle Nearest its assets, founder Fawn Weaver filed a motion to stop the sale. The filing came after Uncle Nearest’s court-appointed receiver Phillip G. Young, Jr., said in a court document on Oct. 9 that the whiskey brand neared sale under Chapter 11.
  • Beloved bev-alc trade show slims after attendance drops: Bar Convent Berlin (BCB), one of the beverage industry’s most influential trade events, will shrink from three days to two days of festivities in 2027 as this year’s attendance dropped by 1,000 visitors and over 100 exhibitors year-over-year. The event’s organizer RX Deutschland said BCB’s trimming-down is part of a broader strategy that will prioritize other in-person trade events of other sizes.

Product releases to watch:

  • Absolut Vodka partners with Charli xcx for product drops, merch: Absolut announced a two-year partnership with the hyperpop icon who made waves with her 2024 album “brat.” The collab will entail limited-edition product drops, branded glassware, and fan activations.
  • Jay-Z and LVMH’s Champagne brand launches a vertical-tasting bundle: Armand de Brignac — also known as Ace of Spades — founded by Jay-Z and now co-owned by LVMH, released a vertical tasting pack for two of its Blanc de Noirs expressions. title: Coors Distributing Co. Is Fighting for Its Life — and the Future of the Middle Tier
summary:

The article Coors Distributing Co. Is Fighting for Its Life — and the Future of the Middle Tier appeared first on VinePair.
content:
In the Mile High City, the fight is on for the future of the middle tier.

A brewer threw the first punch — or at least, the first one in the public eye. In early September, Constellation Brands, the country’s third-largest macrobrewer, told its wholesaler in Denver, Coors Distributing Company (CDC), that it was terminating its arrangement within 30 days. Mark Anthony Group, which ranks fourth behind the Modelo maker in off-premise sales, followed suit less than two weeks later. Sierra Nevada Brewing Company, the country’s second-largest craft brewer by Brewers Association-defined production volume, made its own move for the exit earlier this month.

The dominoes fell so fast, and from a westward territory, that your humble Hop Take columnist heard echoes of Republic National Distributing Company’s collapse in California, which started with rapid-fire departures by major liquor suppliers at the top of 2025, and ended with the mega-distributor’s de facto demise earlier this year. Was it a social contagion? Blood in the water? Something else?

It’s in vogue for beverage-alcohol industry c-suiters to blame abstractions like “headwinds,” and “Zoomers” whenever trouble arises. But my reporting on RNDC’s California cataclysm indicated bad business decisions, institutional arrogance, and infrastructural rot had pushed the firm to the brink right as the hangover in post-Covid booze sales began to bite. There are always causes, and some are always more proximate than others.

So what’s the casus belli for Colorado’s middle-tier trench war? The militants aren’t saying much.

“We’re exploring all legal and commercial options,” CDC tells Hop Take via email. “None of the parties provided any reason for their termination and doing so without cause is a direct violation of the Colorado beer franchise law.” The firm, a wholly owned distributorship of Molson Coors Brewing Beverage Co., has already asked Denver’s district court to enjoin Constellation and Mark Anthony from exiting; it is “evaluat[ing] next steps with Sierra Nevada.”

“We have concluded our partnership with Coors Distributing Company and remain grateful for their partnership over the years,” says Ellie Preslar, Sierra Nevada’s chief growth officer, in an emailed statement. “Though this was a difficult decision, it is necessary for both the long-term and short-term needs of our business.”

A spokesperson for Constellation declined to comment, citing the litigation. Mark Anthony did not respond.

What gives? I doubt it’s frustration over facilities. After all, in a bit of incredibly unfortunate timing, CDC just cut the ribbon on a new state-of-the-art, 70,000 square-foot warehouse at the end of August, less than two weeks before Constellation’s pink slip. If you work at or with CDC, and know more, please get in touch by emailing dave@dinfontay.com or texting dinfontay.11 on Signal. (You can remain anonymous in my coverage.) But in the meantime, tune your ear to another echo of RNDC’s retreat from the Golden State, because suppliers aren’t just leaving CDC — they’re heading to Reyes Beverage Group. Or at least, trying to.

History doesn’t repeat itself, but often rhymes, and it’s rhyming in the Rockies right now. “How much RNDC blood is on Reyes’s hands in California?” I asked in a column the week I broke the news that the now-defunct distributor was exiting the market last year. “Maybe more than you think.” I was never able to verify whether RBG was in talks to acquire RNDC CA before its exit, as some sources had claimed. But there’s no doubt the mighty beer-turned-”total beverage” distributor’s fierce, many-fronted competition in California hastened RNDC’s failure there. Most of the suppliers who fled pre-collapse, fled to RBG.

A few states east and 18 months later, Mark Anthony and Sierra Nevada have signaled their aims to move their CDC volume to RBG. Constellation has been playing coy, but it’s almost unfathomable that it would move to another house. In a remarkable turn of industry fate, RBG acquired its Colorado operation just this year from, you guessed it: RNDC. Its entry into the state, along with Southern Glazer’s Wine & Spirits’ acquisition of Eagle Rock Distributing Co. earlier this year, has shifted the middle-tier calculus there. Now, CDC is facing subtraction.

(Laurel Slick, RBG’s vice-president of corporate affairs, provided statements to Hop Take welcoming Mark Anthony and Sierra Nevada to the fold.)

But. But! While CDC execs may be uttering f-words privately, they’re uttering another f-word publicly: franchise. The history of franchise law is long, winding, and deathly boring, but the upshot is that beer distributors are nearly unique in the protections afforded to them by most states’ laws. The most crucial of these is the so-called “just cause” provision, which requires brewers to cite a legally defensible breach of their agreement with the house they’re trying to terminate. This provision is written into most states’ codes because wholesalers marched on statehouses to make it so in the ‘60s, ‘70s, and ‘80s. Critics argue it harms competition by making it difficult for good brewers to bail on bad distributors; boosters insist it protects competition by making it difficult for bad brewers to strong-arm good distributors. But it’s there.

The protective power of this provision was tested most famously in Florida roughly a quarter-century ago, and distributors came away with the whip hand. In Maris Distributing v. Anheuser-Busch, Inc., a wholesaler fought the brewer tooth and nail for a decade over a termination it believed unjust. The family — the kin of baseball great Roger Maris, who’d been bestowed an A-B house by Gussie Busch after finishing out his Hall of Fame career with the St. Louis Cardinals — won a $120 million settlement in 2005.

As the mantra goes: there are 50 different states, and 50 different three-tier systems. A version of the just-cause clause is on the books in Colorado. But it’s a weird version. It dictates a brewer hoping to terminate a distributor has to cite “alleged noncompliance” and allow the offending firm 60 days to “cure” the infraction. If the distributor doesn’t shape up in that time, then the brewer can ship out. That’s all right at the top of C.R.S. § 44-3-408. But in subsection three, the code appears to contradict itself, noting “the supplier shall have the right to terminate an agreement with a wholesaler at any time by giving the wholesaler at least ninety days’ written notice by certified mail.” To me, a not-lawyer, , the Colorado code appears to say that a brewer must have just cause to terminate a distributor after 60 days, but can terminate for any reason after 90 days.

You will not be shocked to learn that this is not how CDC’s actual lawyers read the text. “Under Constellation’s novel interpretation of Colorado law, its termination will become final after 90 days,” the firm’s legal team wrote in a September 25 filing. “In the interim, there is a likelihood that CDC will face cascading terminations from its other suppliers.”

For a trade that has long grasped the power of a united political bloc, CDC’s existential fight is cause for alarm. At the National Beer Wholesalers Association’s (NBWA) annual conference in Orlando in mid-October, president and chief executive Craig Purser sounded the klaxons. “The efforts to weaken the three-tier system are going to keep coming, and that’s why we need you to double down on your support and participation in NBWA and your state’s association,” he said, per a dispatch from Brewbound.

Whether the suppliers’ assessments of Colorado’s code are innovative, or illegal, is a matter for the judicial system. But in the meantime, if you’re wondering who the hell would write a statute like that, well, the independent beverage-alcohol bar (ahem) is too. Colorado’s franchise law is “really badly written,” Drew Jaglom of Tannenbaum Helpern Syracuse & Hirschtritt LLP told a presumably sympathetic crowd at the NBWA confab, Brewbound reported.

“What good is a statutory right to cure a breach if a supplier can bypass it simply by waiting another thirty days?” asks Ashley Brandt, the Tucker Ellis LLP attorney behind the prolific trade blotter Libation Law Blog, in a post about the CDC brew-haha. “A supplier that cannot establish a breach—or knows the distributor will fix it—could simply choose the ninety-day route. What happens during those additional thirty days that makes a performing distributor’s continued contractual compliance irrelevant?”

It’s a good question. For CDC, it may wind up being the question. And with the pendulum of power lately swinging back towards big suppliers, you can bet the rest of the middle tier will be hanging on the answer.

🤯 Hop-ocalypse Now

Well, Halloween is right around the corner, so it’s a good thing your costume is already covered. What’s that? You’re not wearing the Adult Wedgehead Jumpsuit Costume ($69.99)? The totally epic apparel that corresponds to Shock Top’s Candy Corn Wheat Ale, a new and not-at-all-depressing collaboration between Tilray Brands and retail Grim Reaper Spirit Halloween? Huh. I mean… why not?

📈 Ups…

Stone Brewing co-founders Greg Koch and Steve Wagner are taking over the firm’s recently closed World Bistro & Gardens in Escondido… First-wave craft-brewing pioneer Deschutes will take a crack at the booming “hard sports drink” space with a malt-based offering, Firelyte… Sapporo USA says it has a path to double last year’s volume by the end of 2027… The absolute rubes who bought Ultra Right 100% Woke-Free American Beer back in 2023 still haven’t received it, and Georgia’s attorney general is now investigating, lol… Twin Cities icon Summit Brewing found a new lender to take over its about-to-be-foreclosed-upon loans…

📉 …and downs

Pioneering craft-brewing supplier Admiral Malting announced plans to shutter… Mega-brewers Constellation Brands and Mark Anthony Group are jumping into the “hard sports drink” segment, too — with vodka-based offerings… Centi-billionaire and known freak (but I repeat myself) Mark Zuckerberg finally figured out how to make Guinness look uncool…

summary:
Oysters are a glamorous dish. Often served on a lofty tower over a pile of crushed ice, they gleam and glisten as they await a spritz of lemon juice or dash of mignonette. Pair the bivalves with some Champagne, a salty Sancerre, a crisp Martini, or even a pint of Guinness, and you’re in for a glitzy treat. What’s less glamorous, however, is actually ordering oysters. Whether at a dedicated raw bar with an in-depth oyster menu or a casual restaurant with just a few varieties listed, names like “Blue Point,” “Pemaquid,” and “Bombazine” can seem like a foreign language.

The article The Ultimate Oyster Flavor Map [Infographic] appeared first on VinePair.
content:
Oysters are a glamorous dish. Often served on a lofty tower over a pile of crushed ice, they gleam and glisten as they await a spritz of lemon juice or dash of mignonette. Pair the bivalves with some Champagne, a salty Sancerre, a crisp Martini, or even a pint of Guinness, and you’re in for a glitzy treat.

What’s less glamorous, however, is actually ordering oysters. Whether at a dedicated raw bar with an in-depth oyster menu or a casual restaurant with just a few varieties listed, names like “Blue Point,” “Pemaquid,” and “Bombazine” can seem like a foreign language. And unlike wine lists, which are typically accompanied by a sommelier to guide guests through complex terms, having an oyster expert on deck is a bit less common.

Snapping an Instagrammable pic of the aesthetically arranged half shells is one thing — but getting the exact flavor and texture that you want is another. Depending on the variety and location of origin, oysters bring a wide range of flavors. Before diving into the menu, it can be helpful to decide whether you want creamy, almost sweet oysters or briny ones that taste like a gulp of fresh salt water. Beyond flavor, you should also determine if your preferred texture is meaty and hefty or lean and easy to swallow.

To help make your oyster-ordering experience a bit easier, VinePair tapped Ben Crispin, general manager at Maison Premiere, one of Brooklyn’s most celebrated raw bars, to describe the flavors and textures of 15 different varieties. With his help, we charted the oysters across two scales: briny to creamy and lean to meaty.

Next time you find yourself face-to-face with a menu of unknown oyster varieties, turn to this guide to make sure you know what you’re getting.

summary:

Most customer modifications are welcome and reasonable, and are a normal part of working in kitchens.

The article We Asked 10 Chefs: What’s the Weirdest Dish Modification Request You’ve Received? appeared first on VinePair.
content:
Working in the service industry, one of the biggest parts of the job is to meet the expectations and wishes of guests. In restaurants, hosts and servers are the business’ first point of contact with the patrons. They are tasked with making sure specific needs are met, such as flagging any allergens or grabbing extra utensils. Likewise, chefs also frequently bend to the whims of their customers, whether that be cooking a burger to a certain temperature or removing raw onions from a side salad.

Most customer modifications are welcome and reasonable, and are a normal part of working in kitchens. But occasionally, a request will come through the kitchen that’s just outright bizarre. That’s why we asked 10 chefs from around the country to name the weirdest demands they’ve ever seen on an order ticket.

From marshmallow fluff dolloped onto a steak to a “vegan” egg white omelet, these are the craziest dish modifications that guests have asked for, according to chefs.

The weirdest dish mods chefs have ever received:

  • Marshmallow fluff on everything
  • Deep-fried steaks
  • Prime rib sandwich mixed into farmhouse salad
  • Ground ribeye burger served with packaging labels
  • No ginger, garlic, onion, or cilantro
  • Steak cooked half-rare and half-well done
  • Well-done steak tartare
  • Non-fried fried oyster mushroom sandwich
  • Vegan egg white omelet
  • Well-done tuna tartare
  • Caesar salad without the lettuce
  • Exactly seven French fries
  • Hamburger that isn’t on the menu

“Early on, a family brought their own marshmallow fluff and asked us to put it on everything their kids ate, including the steak, fries, and salad. We did it, and it was the most disgusting thing I’ve ever seen. We’ve also had guests ask us to cook their steak in the deep fryer because they only eat things that are deep-fried.” —Mark Bucher, co-owner, Medium Rare, New York City

“A few months after opening Millstone, we had a guest request one of the more unusual modifications I’ve seen: combining our smoked prime rib sandwich with our farmhouse salad. They wanted everything — the warm, thinly-shaved smoked ribeye, caramelized onions, melted provolone, mixed field greens, seasonal vegetables, and crumbled goat cheese — all chopped up and tossed together with our horseradish aioli as the dressing. Essentially, they turned two completely different dishes into one very unconventional steak salad. Nearly a year into service, it’s still one of the most memorable requests we’ve received.” —Tyler Murray, chef, Millstone, Lexington, Ky.

“One of the strangest modification requests I’ve had was a guest who asked us to grind a ribeye steak to make his burger, replace the fries with a salad, and bring out the original packaging for every ingredient so he could personally verify the allergens. He told us he had both a citrus allergy and a ‘greens allergy,’ and said that the price should be reduced because he wasn’t getting the standard sides. After about 40 minutes of us trying every possible way to accommodate him, he took off his shoes and socks and put them on the empty chair next to him. When we finally explained that there were simply some requests we couldn’t safely or reasonably fulfill, he responded, ‘So the chef is refusing to make my meal?’” —Clinton Snowling, vice president of culinary operations, Parched Hospitality Group, NYC and West Palm Beach, Fla.

“Cilantro, ginger, garlic, and onion are part of every Indian and South Asian dish, especially on Drāvida’s menu. One of the craziest modifications was when a guest walked in and said they cannot eat ginger, garlic, onion, nor cilantro. We still made it happen: We made them two amazing dishes from scratch using spices and herbs that would make the sauces flavorful. Instead of using onions, we used leeks and they enjoyed it.” —Aarthi Sampath, chef and founder, Drāvida, NYC

“I have worked in a variety of styles of kitchens, so I’ve seen some weird stuff. But I think the modification that takes the cake was when someone asked for a flat iron steak cooked half-rare and half-well done. Then, the server came back to the kitchen and said the guest was adamant about it ‘not being cut in half,’ which I still think about it to this day. Thankfully, the guest was eventually receptive to ordering another dish.” —Mikey Miller, chef, Field Note at The Ashbrook Hotel, Frankfort, Ky.

“One of the strangest requests I’ve ever received was for a well-done steak tartare. Considering the dish is traditionally served raw, it definitely caught me and our team off guard. At that point, you’re not really ordering steak tartare anymore, but we did our best to capture the flavors of the dish.” —Adam Plitt, executive chef, Delmonico’s Hospitality Group, NYC

“The weirdest dish modification I’ve ever gotten was when a guest didn’t want anything fried, but still wanted a fried oyster mushroom sandwich. So, I had to roast all the ingredients in the oven. It took significantly longer to make, like upwards 30 minutes for a sandwich that otherwise took less than three minutes to get out. The server that was helping the table tried to direct them to items on the menu that didn’t include any fried elements, but they were set on this particular item and then lectured me on the unhealthiness of frying food. Nonetheless, it was very early in my career, and I didn’t know it would have been much easier to say, ‘No.’” —Haley Duren, executive chef, Long Count, NYC

“We were asked to cook a shared ribeye half-medium rare and half-well done because the couple liked different temperatures. We’ve also gotten ‘medium rare, but closer to rare’ and, my personal favorite, ‘medium rare, but cooked through with no pink.’ Someone also once asked for an egg white omelet with no yolk or cheese because they were vegan. We’ve also had requests for an omelet with no eggs, just mushrooms and spinach.” —Barry Tonks, culinary director, IGC Hospitality, NYC and Orlando, Fla.

“One of the most unusual requests I’ve received was for a tuna tartare, but well done. It caught me off guard because raw tuna is what defines the dish. Of course, every guest has their preferences, but that request has certainly stayed with me. The second of the strangest requests I’ve received was for a Caesar salad without the lettuce, just the croutons, parmesan, and dressing. It turned into more of a Caesar salad-inspired snack, but in a restaurant, part of the fun is figuring out how to make a guest’s request work.” —Antelmo Ambrosio, executive chef, Merchants Hospitality, NYC and Nashville

“Two unusual requests stand out to me. I had one customer who would always order French fries, but insist on exactly seven pieces, no more and no less. Another guest would regularly order hamburgers for the entire table, even though they weren’t on the menu at the seafood restaurant where I worked. He would leave an enormous tip and keep coming back.” —Teddy Kim, culinary director, Oiji Mi and bōm, NYC

content:
This episode of The Buildout is brought to you by Farmer’s Gin. As a bartender, I’m always looking for spirits I’d feel confident pouring and recommending to guests, and Farmer’s Gin is one of them. It delivers exceptional quality at a price that makes it a true workhorse behind the bar or even your home bar. It’s made in Idaho using regenerative, organic certified grain, and grown on a family farm. That approach supports healthier soil, biodiversity, and ultimately better ingredients – which you can taste in the glass. The result is a clean, versatile gin that’s perfect for classics like Martinis and Gimlets, and it’s a bottle you can feel good about supporting. Follow Farmer’s Gin at @farmersgin or visit farmersgin.com.

Corima is the result of one chef’s determination to place the food of Northern Mexico within the same culinary conversation as the French cuisine he first learned to cook. Much of Fidel’s success comes from his passion and ambition, but it also reflects the influence of the mentors and guides who helped shape him along the way.

On this episode of “The Buildout,” Fidel Caballero joins Adam to discuss how he transformed a pandemic-era pop-up into a Michelin-starred destination — one that has already spawned two additional businesses, a bakery and a cocktail bar, in just three years.
